subject: Portfolio assistant fallback
text:
When Gemini fails, the chat assistant on my portfolio still answers, with no AI model at all. It got 92.5% of test questions right.

Without a backup, a failed Gemini call means a recruiter's question gets no answer. So I built one that runs in the browser: every fact on the site (each job, project, skill and certificate) is stored as a short passage, a question is matched to passages by keywords and by meaning, and a small ranking model picks the best one. The answer is that passage with its source, so it can't make anything up.

To test it, I wrote 120 questions a recruiter might ask, including typos and questions it should refuse, like salary, visa status and skills not in my profile. I tuned on 80 and kept 40 aside until the end. The 92.5% is on those 40.

The biggest gain came from teaching it when not to answer. Refusing when the ranking model's confidence is low added 4 points, and fixed refusal topics for pay, work authorization and personal details added 7. Together that is more than the ranking model itself added, 10 points.

Speed was the other problem: the first version took 7.5 s per answer. Shorter inputs and a smaller ranking model brought it to 0.9 s, and its 57 MB of files download only the first time Gemini fails. It still misses some vague questions, like "what has he been working on recently".

So a recruiter who asks about my work gets an answer quoted from my own profile, with its source, even when the AI behind the site is down.

If you've built retrieval over a small set of documents, how do you decide when it should refuse instead of answer?

#MachineLearning #NLP
alt_text: Scatter chart of test questions answered right against download size for each assistant design: keywords only 63 percent at 0 MB, with decline rules 70 percent, MiniLM with the L6 reranker 83 percent at 46 MB, MiniLM with L12 85 percent and 90 percent with decline rules at 57 MB, bge-small with L12 92.5 percent at 68 MB. The shipped design, bge-small with L6, reaches 92.5 percent at 57 MB and about 0.9 seconds per answer.

subject: Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine
text:
An auditor checking a ledger in order opens 1,108 entries to find 90% of the problems. Sorted by my risk score, they open 43.

The ledger is simulated. I generated the entries and planted 47 problems, listed in a separate table that the detection code never reads, so every result can be checked against the right answers.

Each entry gets three checks. Benford's Law: in many real financial datasets about 30% of amounts start with 1, so amounts that break that pattern score higher. An Isolation Forest, a model that flags amounts and tax ratios unlike the rest. And a tax-rate rule that flags any claim whose rate doesn't match its category. The pipeline runs in Dagster, so each step can be rerun on its own.

Scoring each check on its own changed how I read the results. The plain tax-rate rule found 45 of the 47 problems and flagged nothing wrongly. The model found 18, and the rule had already found all 18.

So the rule's 45 flags go first, and every one is a real problem: that alone gets an auditor to 90% in 43 entries. The model and Benford's Law rank the rest, and the 2 problems the rule missed come up at entries 131 and 137 of 1,200.

On a real ledger I would start the same way: measure the simple rules alone first, then use a model to rank what they leave.

How do you get labels for a real ledger when nobody plants the answers?

#DataEngineering #AnomalyDetection
alt_text: Line chart of planted anomalies found against entries opened, on simulated data. In risk order, 90 percent of anomalies are found after 43 entries; in ledger order it takes 1,108. 96 percent less review work for the same 90 percent.

subject: Member Messages QA System: Semantic Search & NER-Based Question Answering
text:
I chose embeddings-based semantic search for member questions, ruling out fine-tuned LLMs, knowledge graphs, and rule-based matching.

To answer natural-language questions about member data, I built an interactive /ask API that ranks unstructured messages by cosine similarity over SentenceTransformer embeddings, combined with spaCy named entity recognition and fuzzy first-name matching.

Retrieving unstructured text can easily pull a message that matches the subject but contains the wrong event details, so the system needed to prove how accurate it was at finding the correct member, message, and answer for a given question.

So I ran eval_qa.py to score 26 hand-written, paraphrased questions against a labelled evaluation set.

The answer was that member identification accuracy reached 100%, while message retrieval accuracy and answer extraction accuracy both reached 96%. The one miss asks for Lorenzo's Thursday booking, where the top-ranked message is his Saturday dinner at The Fat Duck. That result led to a clear threshold: CI fails if answer accuracy drops below 90%.

This system now answers natural-language questions about members directly from unstructured message text.

When your semantic search retriever pulls a message for the wrong day of the week, do you fix that in pre-filtering or during answer extraction?

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

subject: Multi-State Land Use Emissions Analysis
text:
Forecasting emissions by copying last year beats two standard models on real state data.

I built a geospatial ETL system to process daily land-cover data for five U.S. states. The daily files are simulated, but the underlying emission factors and historical inventory come from the EPA. This setup allowed me to test if complex models add value over a simple rule when predicting year-ahead shifts.

The core challenge is that land-use change is often slow. A naive baseline that predicts next year's value as identical to last year's is a strong competitor. To see if learning patterns from history helps more than just repetition, I compared Linear Regression and Random Forest against this baseline.

The test used the EPA's 25 annual series. I trained the models on data up to 2017 and scored their predictions for 2018 through 2022. The Linear Regression reached an accuracy of 0.9418. The Random Forest scored 0.9329. The naive baseline, which simply used the previous year's value, achieved 0.947.

The result was clear: neither model outperformed the simple baseline. The decision was to report the baseline alongside model scores. This ensures that any deployment or further analysis accounts for the fact that historical inertia is the dominant signal in this specific dataset.

#DataEngineering #MachineLearning

subject: Job Market Lakehouse
text:
A June 2025 query on my job market lakehouse read 3,015 of its 60,000 rows. Hive never opened the other 20 months.

I built the lakehouse to learn how a whole data system fits together, from raw files to checked output. With AI changing how work gets done, I think an engineer has to stay broad and keep adapting.

The pipeline runs on simulated job postings from 400 companies. PySpark transforms them, 11 Great Expectations checks gate the output, Airflow runs the steps, and a HiveQL table keeps the raw postings in Parquet, split by month.

Splitting a table that way only saves work if the engine skips the folders a filter rules out, so I tested it. I wrote one month's files straight to storage, registered them with MSCK REPAIR TABLE as the 21st partition, then filtered on June 2025 and read the query plan. The plan pruned to a single partition, and the query returned only June's postings.

So the split pays off where it counts: a one-month question costs 3,015 rows of reading instead of all 60,000, and the plan itself shows it.

#DataEngineering #HiveQL
